1:
Dear Secretary,

Welcome to the company.

From today, one of the most important responsibilities is managing incoming emails safely and effectively. Our business depends on good communication, but it also depends on keeping dangerous messages out of our system. Every email you review could be harmless, urgent, or a threat.

Your task is simple:
Read each email carefully and decide whether it is safe or dangerous.

If an email looks dangerous, delete it immediately.

If an email looks safe, send it forward.
2:
Dear Esteemed coworker,

Congrats on surviving your first day.

As part of keeping the inbox safe, please continue to keep an eye out for possible phishing emails. Here is an additional sign to look out for.

A good check is whether the sender's email address actually matches the company they are pretending to be from. Also, be careful with anything that sounds too good to be true.

You might also experience pop-ups from time to time, so be sure to drag them over to the recycle bin as quickly as possible to prevent them from multiplying.

Now for any links to websites or files, you will not be able to access them, since they might contain personal information about me. Therefore, you will need to evaluate the authenticity of mails without having access to this.

You might also notice a skull pop-up in between, and this sadly means you have sent forward a spam email.

Thanks for helping keep things secure, and good luck on your second day.

Best regards,
Cyber Security team boss
3:
Dear esteemed coworker,

You survived another day, huh? Not many people last that long. I'm proud of you!

But it will only get harder, so be sure to stay on your toes. It seems like phishing emails are growing in how subtle they are, so we've developed further signs to look for to prevent scam emails from coming through.

The first new sign to watch for is generic greetings. Phishing emails now avoid using your real name. While this may seem harmless at first, it can be a clue that the sender does not actually know who you are and may be sending the same message to many people at once.

Another major warning sign is urgency or threats. Scammers will from now on often try to make you panic so you act quickly without thinking, so be sure to look out for this from now on.

Stay alert, stay skeptical, and don't let the phishers win.
4:
Dear esteemed coworker,

You made it to Day 4. Impressive. At this point, the phishers are probably getting nervous.

But don't relax too much. Phishing emails are still out there, and they are getting better at looking normal. Today's new signs to watch for are bad grammar and links or attachments.

The first sign is bad grammar. Many phishing emails include strange wording, spelling mistakes, awkward sentences, or phrases that just don't sound natural. One small mistake does not always mean an email is fake, but several mistakes together can be a major warning sign.

The second sign is links and attachments. Scammers often want you to click a link or open a file so they can steal information, install malware, or trick you into entering passwords. You need to therefore be on the edge for links and check the destination of it before clicking. I've installed a software on the computer, which lets you see the destination of an image or link.

It's also important to note that phishing emails are now only suspicious if they include at least 3 of the signs I've mentioned so far over the days. Anything less than 3 is to be considered a normal email.

I'll give you a list of all the signs mentioned so far in case you forgot:

- Sender email address mismatch
- Offers that sound too good to be true
- Generic greetings
- Urgency or threats
- Bad grammar or strange wording (only if recurrent throughout the mail)
- Suspicious attachments

Stay alert, read carefully, and don't let a messy sentence or suspicious link fool you.

Best regards,
The Cybersecurity Team Boss
5:
Dear esteemed coworker,

You made it to Day 5, which is also your last day! At this point, you are becoming harder to fool, which is exactly what we want.

Today's new sign to watch for is images that look off or out of proportion. The image may be stretched, blurry, oddly cropped, too large, too small, or placed strangely in the message.

This can happen because scammers copy images from real websites and paste them into fake emails. When they do this, the images may not fit correctly. A company logo might look squished or a button might be uneven.

You've been a wonderful coworker, and I have valued your work these past four days. Impress me one last time, and I promise I will put in a good word for you for future jobs.

Also note how it still counts that scam emails have at least 3 of the aforementioned signs, while those under 3 are to be considered non-scam emails and can be safely sent forward.

And if you by some happenstance managed to forget the signs I've mentioned, here is another list:

- Sender email address mismatch
- Offers that sound too good to be true
- Generic greetings
- Urgency or threats
- Bad grammar or strange wording (only if recurrent throughout the mail)
- Suspicious attachments
- Out of proportion images

Best regards,
The Cybersecurity Team
